newsitem.title: USA: Europe not provoking grain price war - EU official.
newsitem.headline: Europe not provoking grain price war - EU official.

text.p: Despite its recent use of export subsidies, Europe has neither the money nor the desire to provoke an international grain price war, a senior EU official said in a speech to be delivered Tuesday at a key agricultural conference.

"Although export refunds have been re-introduced to enable Community exporters to follow the downward movement of world prices, we have neither the budgetary resources nor the intention of provoking a price war," said D.F. Roberts, deputy director general of the European Commission.
The remarks are to be delivered Tuesday at the U.S. Department of Agriculture's annual Agricultural Outlook Forum.

The European Union last fall resumed using subsidies to help push out grain exports. U.S. Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman and other senior administration officials quickly warned Europe that Washington was closely monitoring its moves and would restart the U.S. subsidy programme if necessary.

In comments to state agriculture directors on Monday, Glickman said the administration was seeking full funding in fiscal 1998 of the U.S. subsidy programme -- the Export Enhancement Programme -- to be ready to "fight fire with fire."

Europe is faced with a big budget challenge as governments try to reduce their deficits to levels agreed to in order to participate in Monetary Union, and Roberts said there was no room to expand the EU's farm budget.

"The Farm Budget will be hitting its limits in 1997 and again in 1998, even on existing policies," Roberts said. "Governments are not going to find the budgetary resources to increase these limits when they are all struggling to meet the strict budgetary conditions for participating in Monetary Union."

Roberts said that given Europe's big cereals production last year -- which he estimated at more than 200 million metric tons -- and the current competitive export environment, it will be difficult to increase Europe's export volume.
He said a "significant" rebuilding of grain stocks by the end of the season "seems inevitable."
Roberts said European officials are debating the direction that EU agricultural policy should take for the next decade, and noted there are two predominant schools of thought in Europe.

One school argues for a liberalised policy with less support and the end of production restrictions, while the more traditional view is to maintain current farm structures with prices supports, output controls and import protection.
The official maintained that even large price cuts across the board would not lead to major reductions in European agricultural production.
"They (price cuts) would not drive us off world markets," said Roberts.

Roberts said production control measures have a greater impact on output than price policy, but that such measures can work only with "an adequate level" of import protection, and added that they are difficult to defend unless other major players also have such restrictions in place.
Roberts concluded that in an open trading environment, European farmers have no choice but to compete on the world markets.
